title: Longest Run After Flips
statement: `bits` is a list of `0`s and `1`s. You may change (flip) **at most `k`** of the `0`s into `1`s. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive `1`s you can have after flipping.

examples.explanation: Flip the two 0s at indices 2 and 3: indices 0 to 6 become seven 1s in a row. (Flipping the 0s at indices 3 and 7 only gives six.)
You may not flip anything and there is no 1.

hints.nudge: A stretch can become all 1s exactly when it contains at most k zeros. So the question is about stretches, not about which zeros to flip.
hints.pattern: Sliding window: grow the right end; when the window holds more than k zeros, move the left end forward until it holds k again.
hints.pseudocode:
left = 0; zeros = 0; best = 0
for right in 0..n-1:
  if bits[right] == 0: zeros += 1
  while zeros > k:
    if bits[left] == 0: zeros -= 1
    left += 1
  best = max(best, right - left + 1)
return best
hints.walkthrough: Checking every stretch and counting its zeros costs O(n^2) (or O(n^3) if you recount each time). Notice that the zeros you flip will always be the ones inside the stretch you are looking at, so a stretch is 'good' exactly when it has at most k zeros. Slide a window over the list: move its right end one step at a time and count the zeros inside. When the count exceeds k the window is too greedy, so move the left end forward (reducing the zero count whenever the element leaving is a 0) until the count is k again. The window is always the longest good stretch ending at `right`; keep the largest size seen. Both ends only move forward, so O(n).
